document.title: Afghanistan: The Taliban's Mullah Rabbani: Contender for Taliban Leadership? (Islama 02685)
document.publisher: National Security Archive (GWU), The Taliban Biography: The Structure and Leadership of the Taliban 1996-2002
document.note: [Confidential] Rumors of division between Omar and Deputy Leader Rabbani as Rabbani raises his public profile. State does not expect imminent change given the emphasis on unity. Sources conflict on whether Rabbani is a moderate or backs Omar on gender issues and safe haven for bin Laden. Ghaus and Hassan reportedly losing influence. Excised.

events.description: Establishment of the Taliban movement; Rabbani seen as highest-ranking after Omar
Rabbani represented Taliban at OIC Special Summit in Islamabad
Mullah Ghaus failed to subdue Taliban opponents in Mazar-i-Sharif; Jalil told POLOFF Rabbani had mental problems
Embassy cable on Rabbani-Omar rivalry; contact conversation on Brahimi meeting
Rabbani represented Taliban at OIC Special Summit, meeting over 20 leaders.
Mullah Jalil told US diplomats Rabbani has mental problems.
Ghaus failed to subdue Taliban opponents in Mazar-i-Sharif.
Rumors told to US diplomats that Rabbani was forced into exile by Omar.
Rabbani met Nawaz Sharif, Brahimi, and Bellamy in the two weeks before April 7.
Observers told Embassy POLOFF of Rabbani/Omar tensions.
Conversation between an observer and Embassy Poloff in which the observer said the Taliban are like Bolsheviks focused on party unity and doubted an open Rabbani–Omar split.
A source told Poloff that Rabbani could benefit from Pashtun tribal leadership support as a more tribal man than Omar.
U.S. Embassy Islamabad cable 02685 (Eastham) assessing Rabbani as a possible contender for Taliban leadership.

key_claims: Mullah Rabbani, Taliban deputy leader, raised his public profile in early 1998 as the Taliban's main interlocutor with Pakistan, Saudi Arabia and the UN.
Observers speculated about rival cliques around Rabbani and Omar, but most doubted an open split given Taliban solidarity.
Rabbani's alleged clique included Hassan Akhund, Ghaus, Yar Mohammad, Jalaluddin Haqqani and Nuruddin Turabi, while Omar's included Wakil Ahmed, Hassan Rahmani, Jalil, Khairkhwah and Allahdad.
Some contacts thought Rabbani was more open to negotiating with the northern factions, while others saw only stylistic differences.
One contact said Rabbani supported Omar's safe-haven policy for Usama bin Ladin.
Rabbani made long visits to Saudi Arabia, which Taliban officials cited as evidence of mental or health problems.
Possible long-term scenario: Rabbani could replace Omar after battlefield defeats, backed by Pashtun tribal leaders.
